title: Ignacio Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: See Ignacio well depths, yields, water levels and drilling costs. The median well is 200 feet, with finished costs of $16,000-$27,000.
h1: What Wells Are Like Around Ignacio, Colorado
intro_html:
Buying land near Ignacio means looking closely at the well record before you rely on a contractor’s estimate. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records show 1,317 permitted wells, though only 608 report a total depth, 103 report a pump yield, and 24 report a static water level.

The local record is useful but not complete. It points to a typical well around 200 feet, a median reported yield of 6.0 gallons per minute, and a water level 14 feet below the surface. Those figures help frame a bid and a property investigation, but they do not guarantee what a new well will produce.

sections.heading: How deep are wells near Ignacio?
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Ignacio is 200 feet. The middle half runs from 120 to 250 feet, so a driller estimating a conventional site in this area may reasonably start in that range. The depth mix supports that picture: 16% of wells are under 100 feet, and 66% fall between 100 and 300 feet.

There are important exceptions. Six percent are between 300 and 600 feet, while 11% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 3,698 feet, and the 90th percentile is 2,614 feet. Those outliers show why a flat per-foot allowance is safer than assuming every Ignacio lot will match the median. Ground conditions, the target aquifer, and the success of nearby wells matter.

sections.heading: Expected well yield around Ignacio
sections.html:
Among the 103 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 6.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 2.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. Nearly half, 47%, report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Another 29% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 10% are under 1 gallon per minute and 15% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

For a buyer, that spread is more useful than the median alone. A 6.0-gallon-per-minute well can be workable for household use when the storage and pressure system are properly sized, but a result under 1 gallon per minute deserves careful review. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, and any storage-tank plan. An exempt household-use well is generally subject to a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water levels and the Ignacio trend
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are relatively shallow in this data set. The median depth to water is 14 feet below the surface, and the middle half is 10 to 35 feet. That is a useful starting point for pump planning, trenching, and understanding how much lift the system may need.

The decade figures do not show a simple dropping water table. The median measured level was 25 feet below surface in the 2010s and 14 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later reported measurements are shallower. Only 24 wells report a static water level, however, so this is a limited record rather than a countywide trend. Seasonal conditions, measurement timing, well location, and different wells can all affect the comparison.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Ignacio, and when?
sections.html:
Permit activity is not new around Ignacio. The records include 24 permits from the 1950s, 93 from the 1970s, 127 from the 1980s, 216 from the 1990s, 236 from the 2000s, 458 from the 2010s, and 31 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. That history gives a buyer a substantial group of older neighboring wells to investigate.

The most active drillers in these records are Mortimer Water Well Drilling, with 126 wells; Dak Drilling LLC, with 103; and Beeman Bros Drilling Inc., with 88. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation or proof of current availability. Colorado DWR records can help identify nearby construction reports, but confirm licensing, scheduling, and the proposed scope directly before hiring a driller.

sections.heading: What a new well costs near Ignacio
sections.html:
The cost model for Ignacio assumes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. A typical drilling rate is $50 to $75 per foot. At the local median depth of 200 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $10,000 to $15,000.

A finished system costs more than the hole. Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, the model puts a completed well at about $16,000 to $27,000. Treat this as a planning range, not a guaranteed bid. A lot that requires substantially more than 200 feet, difficult access, additional casing or grout, or special electrical and trench work can move outside it. Ask for a written breakdown that separates drilling from equipment and site work.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Ignacio
sections.html:
Low yield is the clearest measurable risk in the local record: 10% of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute. Dry holes and very deep wells are also possible, as shown by the 2,614-foot 90th percentile and 3,698-foot deepest record. The 1,197 permits naming an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer point to ground where results can be difficult to predict from surface conditions alone.

Environmental review matters too. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 80 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. That does not prove a particular well is contaminated. Test existing water and review nearby site information with the appropriate agencies. Confirm septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, well access, casing and grout details, and building locations before committing to a lot. In an over-appropriated basin, determine whether an augmentation plan is required.

sections.heading: A practical plan for an Ignacio lot
sections.html:
Start with the neighboring wells, not just the listing description. Pull DWR construction reports within the property’s immediate area and compare depths, reported yields, aquifers, water levels, and permit uses. The local data are dominated by domestic or household permits at 56%; stock use is 4%, irrigation is 1%, and monitoring is 2%. A nearby household well is usually more relevant to a home site than an unrelated monitoring well.

Before closing, make the well a due-diligence item. Obtain the permit and construction report, verify the well location, inspect the pump and pressure equipment, and order water testing appropriate to the site history. For a vacant lot, get a driller’s access and depth estimate, price the complete system, and reserve room for the well, septic field, replacement area, driveway, and home. If the proposed use is more than household use, check water rights and augmentation requirements early.

faq.q: How deep are wells near Ignacio, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth within 5 miles of Ignacio is 200 feet, and the middle half runs from 120 to 250 feet. Most recorded wells, 66%, are between 100 and 300 feet. The range is wide, though: 11% exceed 600 feet, the 90th percentile is 2,614 feet, and the deepest record is 3,698 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Ignacio?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 200-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $10,000 to $15,000. A finished system including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $16,000 to $27,000. A deeper hole or difficult site can cost more.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Ignacio?
faq.a: Of the 103 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 6.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 2.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. Ten percent report under 1 gallon per minute. That does not predict a new well by itself, so review nearby construction reports and require clear pump-test information before relying on a supply.

faq.q: Is well water safe near Ignacio, Colorado?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapping shows 80 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory, review local environmental information, and retest after equipment or land-use changes. A nearby site does not automatically mean a specific well is contaminated.

faq.q: What should I check before buying a home with a well in Ignacio?
faq.a: Obtain the Colorado DWR permit and construction report, confirm the well location and permitted use, and inspect the pump, tank, electrical system, and water quality. Compare the property with nearby wells: the local median yield is 6.0 gallons per minute and median water level is 14 feet below surface. Also confirm septic setbacks, access for service, and any augmentation requirement.
